quotes.text: Sometimes you don't speak to each other, and you go in the studio and you just make songs. It's our way of hanging out; we talk about music and make music.

I usually write lyrics when I'm in the club, or when I'm walking home from the club... Like under the influence—there's a lot more real thoughts, and then you wake up and look at the lyrics and you try to understand what you wrote the night before. I don't sit down and say, 'Now I'm gonna write lyrics.'
Making music for us is like having a drunk conversation or a high conversation. It's just something that happens.
I think vibes and human relations are also super, super influential. Just being in a room at a place at night could give me more inspiration than listening to a Chief Keef track or something.
I think it started off as a character. I think Yung Lean was everything Jonathan wasn't... A mixture between like personal and real stuff. That's when I write the best.
I get a lot of inspiration from movies. And Bjork. Anything—even The Knife and stuff. It's so everyday, but it's also colossal.
I'm really into, like, characters—music characters like Sid Vicious and Kurt Cobain, just like how they are and stuff. Like Lil Wayne.
Obviously it's the music mostly—it's the best language.
When you're just listening and you're like, lalalala, and then there's something real, and it's like, Whoa, he's actually a human.
I've come to realise it's better to make music sober.
I used to get so fucked up when I wrote songs, but now I try to get a little bit more sober when I create.

William Burroughs influenced me a lot. It sounds cheesy but I love Naked Lunch. I love And The Hippos Were Boiled In Their Tanks, the one he did with Jack Kerouac. I also love Howl by Allen Ginsberg. The Beat Generation were kind of like Sad Boys. A bunch of people doing the same thing and inspiring each other.
A lot of people think it's easy. They think they can say stupid stuff on a trap beat and make a video with 3D shit in the background. But you can't steal ideas. You have to be original.

It's like an unstoppable force. Sherman and Gud both have ADHD, so I have to be the calm one. Then when we make music I become the crazy one in the booth, jumping around. It's like theatre; we trade positions. They're my friends, they're my family, they're all I have.
Most of the songs are from the heart. If my voice sounds aggressive then it's just from that time and space.
I'm still an outsider in the hip hop community. I don't even know if I'm making hip hop anymore.

Stranger is much easier, a neon, light-blue sound. If Warlord was going through the gates of hell, you would come out the other end into a garden and Stranger is playing with medieval naked people laying in the garden.
That's how it starts. You look at things and people through a lens, and it comes out completely different.
It's very Swedish, with the minimal production. I guess it kinda makes sense. You can't really run from your roots.

It felt like me, Gud, Sherman and White Armor were a band. The process of it was, like... I can't even remember it, 'cause it was just having fun, basically. We were just creating, kinda like jamming, and then out of nowhere we had 14 songs.
It's like reaching really deep into your mind and losing control between what's real and what's not.
You're expressing yourself in the purest art forms, painting and singing.
'Stranger' was my Pet Sounds. I guess it can get better, but to me I feel it was quite a big point in my career.

I guess it kinda changes monthly, or even daily, and then falls into the same box. Sometimes I can be only listening to Percy Sledge, Al Williams, maybe the Talking Heads. Then it'll be Three 6 Mafia, Young Buck. I guess it all falls into one box of inspiration.
I don't really like when there's guitars and trap drums, like an emo rap song. I think you should go all the way with it. It sounds conservative but the blend just sounds too modern and forced.
It's strange to talk about Talking Heads and Young Buck as being the same but they really are. They both paved the way in their respective genres. They both kinda have the same attitudes.

It's more childish than my music. My music is more developed quite a lot. It's kind of caught up with my years. While my painting's still at the Jonathan level. I've had no education in painting, so that's why.
We were thinking that we should really take our time making something that sounds like a Fleetwood Mac album. Kind of like expansive and polished, and really write songs.

Releasing stuff isn't the most fun because you've already done the work. You're just kind of sitting on your ass waiting to get to the next chapter. But I want to learn how to be in the project for a little longer, and like, stay there. Maybe even celebrate, not just always move on to the next [project].
I think in my head all of our worlds kind of collide. I'm not too aware of what kind of fan bases exist. I just think about artists who would be good to have on a song together.
I don't think putting everyone in special boxes just so their fans are happy is a good way to do it. I think you should just mix it, you know?

You split it up. You make names for things. Me and whitearmor we sat down and would say, "This is album worthy, this is mixtape worthy, this is EP worthy, this is 'work on,' this is trash, this is maybe a good idea, this is maybe a bad idea."

Everything is from scratch, so. whitearmor and Yung Sherm Portugal, they'd wake me up with a cup of coffee and then they would go downstairs and start playing something on the piano. Then whitearmor might say we should record this or that, then he'd put a synth over it and then I'd start singing. Then I'd start recording a melody on my iPhone. Everything is very intuitive and you get into this workflow.

I think we had a lot more rules when we were younger, we wanted songs to be specific and a beat to be made and all these rules of how it should sound. whitearmor, Sherm, and Gud they can play guitar, they can play piano, they can play anything. Right now we're just messing around with it all, you know?

If you put yourself out in a lot of costumes — lets say you would go and dress up and make three different characters, then maybe you would be more honest in that costume than you would be without the costume, you know what I mean? Sometimes while going for a new alias or a new musical genre or just experimenting, you're more honest than you would be if you're just yourself.

I'm really glad if I can help people to do exactly that with music or art or whatever that you just dress up, make a character, and just start going in. Because you'll find out so much about yourself and what you're interested in and why you're interested in that.

Everyone's desires come up in their art, and if they come out in their art it's much better. People can have terrible lives. They could have been killers, but if they make a song, maybe that's like their purest part of their soul.
Creating is the only thing that's keeping me sane, to be honest.

You've got to be fearless. You have to provoke something. It doesn't have to be provocative in that sense, but you have to provoke someone's feelings or something, you know. You have to get someone to feel something. And if they feel hate? I'm happy. And if they feel love? I'm happy. They're both very strong emotions. But if they say it's just okay, I can't stand it.

When there's a certain energy in the room and you've had it in your head for a long time, you want to express that. When I was younger, when I was like 17 or 18 — you know you're young, you're in a big city, you're interested in bleak things and life is bleak and shit goes wrong. Now it hasn't been wrong for a while, so I'm trying to put that out there. You can't fake the funk.
If you bloom into a new flower, you have to express that new flower. You can't be that old, bleak flower.
The name is just my name, Jonatan. I'm trying to break the fourth wall of Yung Lean and Jonatan, and just come together.
I would say it's like an uncle album. It's guitar, straight-from-the-heart songs.
I come from hip-hop, so it's always going to be hip-hop melodies, but more me trying to do, like, Bruce Springsteen.
I'm a poet who does different genres. If I do pop, then it's a poet doing pop, and if I do rock, it's a poet doing rock.
I'm far from the American rapper-core. I can't fake that. I grew up listening to Wu-Tang, and everything that you grew up listening to as well.
For me, it was always writing lyrics and poetry and rapping, and then singing. Then everything came through that.
It becomes little branches on a tree that just grows and grows into this big tree. It pays off to learn one craft.
